units.translation: HERALD: I forbid you to force this city. ANTIGONE: I forbid you to make excessive proclamations to me.
to your brother who is being slandered
Stretch forth a mournful, wretched voice.
Send forth a mournful, all-lamenting, discordant voice.
What is this cry you will utter?
Thus Bergk corrected for αὔδασον [speak!] (αὐδᾶσον [speak!] Schuetz), which is read in Philo vol. 2 p. 468. φωνῆεν φηγοῦ τῆς Δωδωνίδος ξύλον [the speaking oak of Dodona] said Apollodorus 1, 9, 16.
Where is the sacred speaking oak of Argos?
where now from the apograph: αὐθάδη φρονῶν [being self-willed in mind].
the stubborn jaw of the wedge
Do not think that I am silent out of luxury or self-will.
For self-will in one who thinks wrongly is by itself no less strong than anything.
Do not reproach me for my self-will.
Do not ever consider self-will better than good counsel.
to abandon self-will and seek wise counsel
Indeed, even before, by such acts of self-will you brought yourself into these misfortunes.
Concerning murder committed by one's own hand
to wear out another generation with deaths by murderers
There could not be a murder by a kinsman perpetrator.
on that very day, on the same day
On the accent αυθημερόν [on the same day] (not αὐθήμερον [on the same day], as sometimes written in the books) see Ioann. Alex. Τον. παραγγ. p. 30, 25.
on the same day having fenced their bodies with bronze armor
in a torn and corrupt passage, where in M these letters remain
... there ... I utter a mournful cry
at another time, in the future
May they not take it and then flourish again.
to care that it never again rises
Alas, again, struck a second time.
and having nurtured it, again receives a wave of these things
Who is inside, O child, child, again, in the house?
Speak again, so that I may understand more clearly.
Alas, again, in the third address.
An Argive man again dwells in his ancestral wealth.
A dappled wing will again flutter around him.
and again coming to your kinsman
To the gods again, O woman, I will pray.
all who enter the court of Zeus
in the places of Aulis with back-flowing waves
It is a long narrow ditch.
channels: places in a straight line. Aeschylus (fr. 341) also calls the trench and the pyre
to which he adds the very verses of Aeschylus, which see fr. 341.
to increase in no way the ancestral wealth
having the power of increasing, apt to give growth
Thus strength increases greater for mortals.
